title: The land of the enchantresses
hookLine: tradition says Mardana was bewitched in a far country and Nanak's singing set him free

lines: SONGS GET IN WHERE ARGUMENTS DON'T.
cards: A song comes on in a shop, and the man at the till starts humming without noticing. Hours later, at home, the tune is still with him. A friend hums a grandmother's lullaby, and a grown woman is suddenly six years old.
Songs get into people in ways arguments rarely do. The janamsakhis knew that.
Mardana, the Guru's companion, was a musician, and in today's sakhi he gets into trouble in a far country, the kind no argument can get him out of.

teach.b: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana come to a country ruled by women, a land well-known for magic. Mardana, hungry, goes ahead to find food, and doesn't come back. A woman there has cast a spell on him.

Some tellings say she turned him into a ram, tied up with a thread. Others simply say he lost himself, forgot who he was and why he'd come. Nanak goes looking, and finds his friend bound and bewildered.
And the Guru doesn't argue with the spell. He sings.
Tradition says the sound of the Guru's hymn broke the enchantment, and Mardana came back to himself.

teach.h: THE GURU SINGS, THE SPELL BREAKS.
teach.b: Then the women of that land try their arts on Nanak: charms, threads, spells, and in some tellings riches and beauty offered by their queen. None of it holds him. He keeps singing.
And the tellings end with the enchantresses listening, and changed. So what does this story know? Some hear a plain wonder: the Guru's power over magic.
Some readers also hear quieter spells in it: the pull of wanting, of distraction, of forgetting who you are.
The Gurus' hymns have a name for that pull: maya. And the story's answer isn't a lecture.
It's kirtan, the singing of the Guru's word, the same singing that fills a gurdwara today. Mardana's own instrument, the rabab, sits at the beginning of that song.

how: Sikhs gather in gurdwaras for kirtan, singing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib together, and tell this sakhi as a picture of the Guru's word breaking the spells of maya.

games.q: you're Nanak. your friend is under a spell in a strange land, bound and bewildered. what do you do?
o: argue with the woman who cast it.
games.why: tradition says the Guru sang, and the sound broke the enchantment. the tellings end with the enchantresses listening, and changed.

practice: Let a song come to mind, a hymn if you have one, a lullaby, any tune that once brought you back to yourself, and hum it under your breath or just hear it inside.
Then think of someone who seems stuck today under some spell of gloom or worry, and hold them in the tune for a while. If you pray, you can let the tune carry Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan, the Guru's singing that, in the sakhi, broke the spell on Mardana in a far country and set him free.
